summary.text: The active site is the region of an enzyme where substrate molecules bind and undergo a chemical reaction.
It is made of residues that temporarily bind the substrate and residues that catalyse the reaction, and it takes up only about 10–20% of the enzyme.
Its arrangement of amino acids suits one particular substrate and reaction, which gives the enzyme high specificity.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: Usually three to four amino acids

facts.label: Usual shape
facts.value: A groove or pocket, sometimes deep in a tunnel

facts.label: Models of fit
facts.value: Lock and key, induced fit and conformational selection

items.prompt: An enzyme's active site processes one substrate molecule after another. Why can it keep going?

options.label: It swaps in fresh amino acids every time
Its residues are regenerated by the end of each reaction
It stays permanently bound to the product
It draws new energy from the surrounding water

items.explain: An active site can catalyse repeatedly because its residues may change during the reaction but are regenerated by the end.

items.prompt: An inhibitor fits tightly into an active site, yet the enzyme does nothing to it. Why is that a problem for the lock-and-key idea?

options.label: It predicts the active site changes shape to fit
It predicts inhibitors can only bind away from the site
It predicts substrates bind outside the active site
It predicts a tight fit should mean high catalytic efficiency

items.explain: Lock and key says a perfect fit gives high efficiency, yet methylglucoside fits tightly into its enzyme and no reaction occurs.

items.prompt: A hand slides into a glove, and the glove changes shape to fit. Which model of substrate binding does that picture?

options.label: Induced fit
Lock and key
Conformational selection
Active-site saturation

items.explain: The induced fit model assumes a flexible active site that changes shape until the substrate is bound, like a glove fitting a hand.

items.prompt: A cook heats an enzyme far too much and it stops catalysing. What most likely happened to it?

options.label: Heat used up its active-site residues
Heat gave it a second active site
Heat disrupted the interactions holding its shape
Heat turned its binding site into a catalytic one

items.explain: Interference such as high temperature disrupts the interactions that keep the enzyme folded, so it denatures and loses its catalytic activity.

items.prompt: A substrate's charges don't line up with the charges in the active site. What is the result?

options.label: They bind even more tightly
A repulsive force pushes them apart
The substrate gains a second binding site
The enzyme gains a second active site

items.explain: The charge distributions must be complementary, otherwise a repulsive force pushes them apart.

items.prompt: A DNA polymerase's active site is made to grip its substrate more tightly. What is believed to happen to copying accuracy?

options.label: Copying becomes more accurate
Copying becomes less accurate
Copying stops entirely
Accuracy stays exactly the same

items.explain: A tighter fit is believed to increase efficiency, and tighter DNA polymerase binding raises the fidelity of DNA replication.
